newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jerusalem bombs heighten dilemma for Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem bombs heighten dilemma for Arafat.

text.p: When squads of Islamic suicide bombers brought death to Israel last year, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat responded with a crackdown on hundreds of suspected Moslem militants.

Now, analysts say, the former revolutionary leader who sold his people peace with Israel and the promise of a state of their own, may find it harder to mount a similar assault in the wake of Wednesday's carnage in Jerusalem's main Jewish market.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu halted a planned resumption of stalled peace talks in response to the bombings and accused Arafat of failing to arrest the militants.

His right-wing government has said that unless Arafat acts, it will go into Palestinian self-rule areas to do the job itself, a warning Palestinian officials said on Thursday would inflame the situation and risk yet more bloodshed.

"A weakened Palestinian Authority cannot try to stop violence in the way Israel wants it," said Khalil Shkaki, director of the Centre for Palestine Research and Studies in the West Bank town of Nablus.
"It would be discredited in the eyes of its own people," he said.
Wednesday's double suicide bombing, which killed 13 people, was the deadliest against Israel since February-March 1996 when 57 people died in similar attacks by the Islamic militant movement Hamas.

The crackdown Arafat orchestrated following the 1996 killings occurred amid grass roots Palestinian optimism that interim peace deals he had signed with previous Labour Israeli governments were bearing fruit.

The mood in the West Bank and Gaza Strip has since shifted to pessimism, a reverse Palestinians attribute to Netanyahu's Jewish settlement building which has contributed to a virtual standstill in peace negotiations since March.

"There is no culture of peace after one year of this government. Instead there is a culture of fear for the future," said Mahdi Abdul Hadi, head of the Palestinian Academic Society for the Study of International Affairs.
"The only way to stop them (bombings) is to deliver something," he said.
Israeli analysts also saw Arafat caught in a dilemma at a time when his Authority's popular legitimacy is being eroded by allegations of corruption and mismanagement.
"He is almost caught between two conflicting imperatives," said Mark Heller, senior research associate at Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies.
"One is to restrain these people (militants) so they don't put things off course. The other is to avoid a confrontation that gets close to out-and-out civil war," he said.
Netanyahu won election in the wake of the 1996 bombings on a pledge to give Israelis stunned by the killings peace with security.

Wednesday's bloodshed in the heart of Jerusalem, coupled with Netanyahu's allegations that Arafat has let loose militants to "prowl our streets", has touched a raw nerve in an Israel where security is the paramount concern.

"Each (suicide bombing) is not as significant as people think. But the cumulative weight is to cast serious doubt among Israelis as to whether we really have a serious partner in Arafat," said Professor Efraim Inbar, director of the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies in Tel Aviv.
Like other analysts, he said Wednesday's attacks had dealt a serious blow to the peace process at a time of cautious indications that some movement might have been at hand.
Palestinian and Israeli experts alike said the bombings would not kill the process outright.
"No Israeli government has ever been able to enter into serious negotiations in the immediate aftermath of a terrorist attack like this, and certainly not this Israeli government," said Heller.
But he added that with time "everybody goes back to the same game because it's the best one in town."
